questions.q: An ORM loads 50 blog posts, then lazily fetches each post's author inside a loop. How many queries typically execute?
questions.explanation: That is the classic N+1 shape: one query fetches the 50 posts, then one lazy author lookup fires per post, giving 1 + 50 = 51 queries.

questions.q: Which change most directly eliminates an N+1 pattern when loading orders with their customers?
options: Eager-load the association via a join or batched IN query
Add an index on the customers table primary key column
Wrap the per-order lookups inside a single database transaction
Increase the connection pool so the lookups run in parallel
questions.explanation: Eager loading collapses the per-row lookups into one join or one batched IN query. Indexes and bigger pools only make each of the N round trips cheaper, not fewer.

questions.q: EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan on a 50-million-row table for a highly selective WHERE clause. Most likely explanation?
options: The optimizer preferred parallel workers over index access for speed
No usable index exists on the filtered column
Row-level locks are forcing the planner to avoid the index
The filter predicate is being applied after aggregation
questions.explanation: A highly selective predicate is exactly the case an index wins, so a full scan almost always means no index covers that column, or none the predicate can use.

questions.q: Why can SELECT * hurt performance even when the WHERE clause is fully indexed?
options: It disables statistics collection for the optimizer on that table
It acquires broader read locks than a column list would
It always bypasses the shared buffer cache on reads
It drags unneeded columns, blocking index-only scans
questions.explanation: Requesting every column forces heap lookups the index alone could have satisfied, and ships extra bytes over the wire. Locking and caching behavior are unchanged.

questions.q: Where do the row estimates in an EXPLAIN plan come from?
options: Statistics collected by ANALYZE-style sampling of the table
A fast count(*) the planner executes before optimization begins
The row counts observed during the previous execution
The table's file size divided by the average row width
questions.explanation: The planner uses stored statistics (histograms, distinct counts, null fractions) gathered by sampling during ANALYZE. It never touches the data while planning, so stale stats mean bad estimates.

questions.q: When is one JOIN query clearly better than several separate queries?
options: When the tables live on different physical shards
When the join would duplicate each parent row thousands of times
When related rows are needed together on indexed keys
When the application already caches each row individually
questions.explanation: With indexed join keys and rows that are always consumed together, one join beats several round trips. Cross-shard joins and heavy parent-row duplication argue the other way.

questions.q: A composite B-tree index exists on (customer_id, created_at). Which query can use it efficiently?
options: WHERE created_at > now() - interval '7 days'
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
WHERE created_at = '2026-01-01' OR customer_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 with no filter at all
questions.explanation: A composite B-tree is ordered by its leading column first, so equality on customer_id plus a range on created_at seeks straight to a contiguous slice. Predicates skipping customer_id cannot.

questions.q: What is the standard fix for N+1 queries inside GraphQL field resolvers?
options: Persisted queries compiled ahead of time on the server
Response caching for the whole query at the CDN edge
Schema stitching so each service resolves its own fields
Per-request dataloaders that batch and dedupe key lookups
questions.explanation: A DataLoader collects keys requested during a tick, dedupes them, and issues one batched fetch, turning N resolver calls into a single query. Its cache is scoped per request to avoid stale data.

questions.q: A read query got slower right after you added an index it now uses. Most likely cause?
options: Indexes slow all reads once tables pass a certain size threshold
The planner picked the low-selectivity index over a cheaper scan
The index doubled the row count the query must visit
New indexes invalidate the buffer pool until it rewarms fully
questions.explanation: If the indexed column is not selective, the index path matches most rows and adds random heap fetches on top, costing more than the sequential scan the planner used before.

questions.q: Logs show one query for users, then 200 identical queries differing only by user_id. Best immediate fix?
options: Batch them into one query with WHERE user_id IN (...)
Add an index on user_id so each individual lookup gets faster
Move the whole loop into a database stored procedure
Turn on statement caching so repeats skip the parser
questions.explanation: The cost is 200 round trips, so batching the ids into one IN query removes 199 of them. Indexing or statement caching shaves each trip but leaves the count unchanged.

questions.q: A join of two large tables shows a nested loop with a sequential scan on the inner side. What should you check first?
options: Whether the outer table needs vacuuming to clear dead tuples
Whether work_mem is set too high, biasing toward nested loops
Whether the inner table's join column has a usable index
Whether the join should become a UNION of two separate scans
questions.explanation: A nested loop rescans the inner side once per outer row, so a missing index on the inner join column turns the join quadratic. Indexing it makes each inner lookup a cheap seek.

questions.q: Fetching one post plus its 5,000 comments with a single JOIN mainly risks what, versus two queries?
options: Losing snapshot consistency between the two result sets
The optimizer refusing index use across the joined tables
Row locks held on all comments for the query duration
The post's wide columns transferred 5,000 times over the wire
questions.explanation: A one-to-many join repeats every parent column on each child row, so a wide post body is sent 5,000 times. This cartesian bloat is why two queries can win here.

questions.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimated 100 rows but actual 2 million at a filter node. Most productive response?
options: Lower the planner's random_page_cost until the plan changes shape
Pin the current plan with optimizer hints permanently
Refresh statistics; add extended statistics for correlated columns
Partition the table on the filtered column right away
questions.explanation: A four-order-of-magnitude misestimate points at bad or missing statistics, often correlated predicates the planner multiplies independently. Fix the estimate and the plan usually fixes itself.

questions.q: Eager loading is configured, yet N+1 queries persist in production. Which pattern explains this?
options: The template iterates the preloaded association collection more than once
Per-item scoped queries that bypass the preloaded association
The parent rows are iterated twice within one request
The association is serialized to JSON after being loaded
questions.explanation: Adding a scope, filter, or ordering to an association inside the loop produces a different query than the one preloaded, so the ORM discards the cache and hits the database per item.

questions.q: 95% of rows have status 'active'. Why does the planner skip the status index for WHERE status = 'active'?
options: Reading most rows via the index costs more than scanning
B-tree indexes store repeated values poorly beyond a threshold
String equality comparisons cannot use B-tree indexes at all
The index serves only ORDER BY clauses, never WHERE filters
questions.explanation: At 95% selectivity the index path would read the index plus nearly every heap page in random order, which is more expensive than one sequential pass over the table.

questions.q: Wrapping 200 small SELECTs in one transaction barely helps latency. Why?
options: Transactions disable the buffer cache to guarantee consistency
The isolation level forces each read to re-check row visibility
The pool must revalidate the connection for every statement
Each statement still pays a network round trip plus parse cost
questions.explanation: A transaction only saves the implicit begin/commit overhead; the 200 round trips and per-statement parse and plan work remain. Batching or pipelining is what removes them.

questions.q: A request runs 1 parent query plus 100 child queries; each takes 1 ms server-side over a 2 ms round-trip network. Roughly how much latency does collapsing to 2 queries save?
options: About 300 ms saved per request
About 100 ms saved per request
About 30 ms saved per request
Almost nothing, since the database overlaps the requests
questions.explanation: Each child query costs 1 ms plus 2 ms of round trip, so 100 of them cost about 300 ms sequentially. Collapsing to one batched child query reclaims nearly all of it.

questions.q: Postgres chooses an index-only scan, yet still reads heap pages. Why?
options: Index-only scans are restricted to primary key indexes only
Pages not marked all-visible require heap visibility checks
TOASTed values force heap access for every matched row
The executor always verifies the first row on the heap
questions.explanation: Indexes carry no visibility information, so Postgres consults the visibility map. Pages not yet marked all-visible, typically because vacuum has not caught up, force a heap fetch per row.

questions.q: You replace an N+1 with one SELECT ... WHERE id IN (list of 10,000). What new problem can appear?
options: The database silently truncates IN lists at 1,000 entries
IN predicates always degrade to full sequential scans
Plan quality and protocol parameter limits degrade with huge lists
Result ordering becomes tied to the transaction snapshot instead
questions.explanation: Very large IN lists blow up planning time, can exceed bind-parameter limits, and may flip the planner to a scan. Chunking into batches of a few hundred to a thousand is the usual fix.

questions.q: WHERE lower(email) = $1 ignores the B-tree index on email. Which fix actually works?
options: Rewrite the predicate as email = upper($1) so the index applies
Replace the B-tree with a hash index on the email column
CLUSTER the table physically on the existing email index
Create an expression index on lower(email), or use citext
questions.explanation: Wrapping a column in a function makes the predicate non-sargable against a plain index. Indexing the same expression, lower(email), or switching to citext restores index matching.
